title: Juniper Networks Certified Associate Junos (JNCIA-Junos JN0-105)

nodes.title: Access control lists: Key Ideas
nodes.content: An ACL is an ordered list of permit/deny rules evaluated top-down until first match. Used everywhere: router interfaces, switch ports, NTFS files, cloud network ACLs. Order matters — a permit at line 5 won't fire if a deny at line 3 matches the same traffic.

flashcards.front: Standard vs extended ACL — what's the difference?
flashcards.back: Standard ACL (Cisco IOS 1-99): matches source IP only. Extended (100-199 or named): matches source IP + destination + protocol + port. Use extended for anything realistic — standard ACLs can't say 'block SSH from this subnet to that host'. Apply extended close to the source, standard close to the destination.

Every ACL has an invisible `deny ip any any` at the end. If nothing matches your permit rules, traffic is dropped. Common gotcha: configure 'permit ssh from 10.0.0.0/24', forget that this blocks DNS, NTP, ICMP — anything you didn't explicitly permit. Always log the implicit deny while testing to see what you accidentally blocked.

flashcards.front: Inbound vs outbound — which direction to apply?
flashcards.back: Inbound: filter traffic ENTERING the interface BEFORE the router routes it. Outbound: filter traffic LEAVING after the router decided where it's going. Inbound is more efficient (drops bad traffic before routing); outbound is rarely needed except for specific egress filtering. When in doubt, apply inbound on the closest interface to the source.

flashcards.front: Why does order matter in an ACL?
flashcards.back: Rules are evaluated top to bottom; first match wins. If you put 'deny 10.0.0.0/24' before 'permit 10.0.0.5', host .5 is denied — its specific permit never gets reached. Order most-specific rules first, broad rules last. Always end with explicit denies that log, so you can see what's getting blocked.

statements.text: It evaluates each packet independently against `from`/`then` terms based on header fields describes a stateless firewall filter in Junos OS.
statements.explanation: Junos stateless firewall filters (analogous to ACLs on other platforms) are made of ordered terms, each with `from` match conditions on header fields (addresses, ports, protocol, DSCP, etc.) and a `then` action (`accept`, `discard`, `reject`, `count`, `policer`). Each packet is judged on its own — there is no session table — which is why they are called stateless. Connection tracking, return-flow inspection and L7 inspection are jobs for the SRX stateful security policy, not stateless filters. Stateless filters can be applied on any interface, including the lo0 interface to protect the Routing Engine, but their use is not restricted to lo0.

`commit confirmed <minutes>` activates the candidate immediately but starts a timer; if you do not issue a plain `commit` within that window the device automatically rolls back to the previous configuration. This protects against locking yourself out after a risky change. `commit check` only validates syntax without activating anything, `commit synchronize` pushes the configuration to both Routing Engines on a dual-RE chassis, and `commit and-quit` activates the configuration and leaves configuration mode but provides no auto-revert.

statements.text: Routing policy that imports or exports routes between the routing table and protocols is described as a protocol-independent property — meaning it can act on routes regardless of which routing protocol learned them.
statements.explanation: Junos routing policy and routing options (aggregate, generated, static, martians, autonomous-system) are configured under `[edit routing-options]` and `[edit policy-options]`, and they apply to the routing table regardless of where a route was learned. The same policy framework filters BGP advertisements, OSPF redistribution and static-to-IS-IS leaks alike. OSPF summarization, BGP attribute changes and PIM RP election are all features of specific routing protocols, so they are by definition protocol-dependent, not protocol-independent.

nodes.title: Command-line tooling: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Most exam workflows involve `aws`, `az`, `gcloud`, or `kubectl`. Knowing the structure of each (resource → command → flags) saves you in the lab portion and in real life. They're all roughly the same shape with different naming conventions.

flashcards.front: How do you authenticate the AWS CLI?
flashcards.back: `aws configure` writes credentials to `~/.aws/credentials` (access key + secret) and `~/.aws/config` (region, output format). Use named profiles for multi-account: `aws s3 ls --profile prod`. Prefer `aws configure sso` or temporary STS credentials over long-lived access keys.

flashcards.front: What does `kubectl get` do, and what flags are essential?
flashcards.back: Lists resources of a kind: `kubectl get pods`, `kubectl get nodes`. Key flags: `-n <namespace>` (default is `default`), `-o wide` (more columns), `-o yaml` (full manifest), `--watch` (live updates), `-l label=value` (filter by label).

AWS / Azure / gcloud all support `--output json|text|table|yaml`. JSON is for piping into `jq` for scripts. Table is for humans browsing in the terminal. Always set a default in your config so you don't squint at JSON when browsing.

flashcards.front: How do you find a command's options without leaving the terminal?
flashcards.back: `aws <service> <command> help` (or `--help`), `kubectl <verb> --help`, `az <group> <command> --help`. These open built-in docs with every flag listed. Searching the official web docs is for concepts; for syntax, the local help is always current.

nodes.title: IP routing: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Routing is how packets find their way through a multi-network internet. Every router runs a forwarding table; routing protocols (OSPF, EIGRP, BGP) are the mechanisms by which routers exchange information and build that table.

flashcards.back: When multiple routes match a destination, the router picks the one with the most-specific (longest) prefix. So `10.0.0.0/24` beats `10.0.0.0/16` for a packet to `10.0.0.5`. This is how more-specific routes can override defaults.

It matches every destination, so it's used only when no more-specific route exists. Typically points to the internet gateway. On a stub network, the default route is often the ONLY route — everything not local goes 'up' to a smarter router.

flashcards.front: Static vs dynamic routing — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Static routes are hand-configured, easy to understand, perfect for small or stub networks. Dynamic routing (OSPF, BGP, EIGRP) auto-discovers topology, reacts to link failures, scales to thousands of routers. Use dynamic the moment the topology is non-trivial or expected to change.

When the same destination is learned from multiple sources (static + OSPF + BGP), the router prefers the one with the lowest administrative distance. Defaults (Cisco): connected=0, static=1, EIGRP=90, OSPF=110, BGP=200. It's the tie-breaker before the routing-protocol metric.

questions.q: A Junos router learns the prefix 172.16.0.0/16 from a static route, from OSPF internal, and from BGP. Using default route preference values, which source is installed as the active route?
choices: BGP, because external routing information always wins over locally configured routes
OSPF, because link-state protocols are always preferred over static configuration
The static route, because its default preference (5) is numerically lowest
All three are installed and the router load-balances across them equally
questions.explanation: Junos selects the route source with the lowest preference value: static routes default to 5, OSPF internal to 10, and BGP to 170. The static route therefore becomes active. Lower-preference wins is the opposite intuition of 'bigger is better' and is a standard JNCIA test point; equal-cost load balancing only applies to multiple routes from the same protocol at the same preference and metric.

questions.q: On a Junos router, which type of traffic is processed by the Packet Forwarding Engine WITHOUT involving the Routing Engine?
choices: An SSH session terminating on the router's management interface
Transit packets being forwarded from one interface to another
Routing protocol updates such as OSPF hellos addressed to the router
Ping packets whose destination is one of the router's own addresses
questions.explanation: The PFE forwards transit traffic in hardware using its copy of the forwarding table; the RE is not in the data path. Traffic addressed to the router itself — SSH to the management plane, routing protocol packets, pings to local addresses — is exception (host-bound) traffic punted to the Routing Engine. Separating these planes is the core of the Junos architecture.

questions.q: In the output of `show route`, what does an asterisk (*) next to a route entry indicate?
choices: The route has been manually pinned by an operator and cannot be replaced
The route is hidden and excluded from the forwarding table until its next hop resolves
The route is currently active and is the one installed in the forwarding table
The route was learned within the last 60 seconds and is still being verified
questions.explanation: The asterisk marks the active route — the entry chosen among all sources for that prefix and pushed to the forwarding table. Hidden routes are shown by `show route hidden` and carry no asterisk; Junos has no concept of operator-pinned or probation routes in this display.

questions.q: You have a saved configuration file and want to completely replace the candidate configuration with the file's contents before committing. Which command do you use?
choices: load merge /var/tmp/golden.conf
load override /var/tmp/golden.conf
load set /var/tmp/golden.conf
load replace /var/tmp/golden.conf
questions.explanation: `load override` discards the entire candidate and substitutes the file's contents — the full-replacement operation. `load merge` adds the file's statements on top of the existing candidate; `load set` reads a file of set/delete commands and applies them line by line; `load replace` substitutes only the hierarchies marked with `replace:` tags in the file.

questions.q: While typing a command, a Junos operator presses the `?` key after `show interfaces`. What does the CLI do?
choices: Lists the possible completions and options valid at that point in the command hierarchy
Executes the command immediately with default arguments applied to every interface
Opens the full Junos manual page for the show interfaces command family in a pager
Inserts a literal question-mark character into the command line for use in regular expressions
questions.explanation: Context-sensitive help is built into the Junos CLI: `?` at any point lists the keywords, options and arguments valid at that position, with one-line descriptions. It does not execute anything or open manuals. (Spacebar and Tab complete partially typed keywords — another JNCIA staple.)

questions.q: Which command begins the installation of a new Junos OS software package on a device?
choices: copy tftp flash followed by boot system flash
set system software upgrade package jinstall.tgz
request system software add jinstall.tgz
install junos package jinstall.tgz commit
questions.explanation: Software operations in Junos are operational-mode `request` commands: `request system software add <package>` validates and installs the package, typically followed by `request system reboot`. `copy tftp flash` is Cisco IOS practice; software installation is not a configuration statement, so no `set` syntax applies; there is no `install junos` command.
